# Research

Research answers questions that routine coverage cannot resolve.

## Purpose

Research uses a stated method to produce an original finding. Its evidence may
come from data, documents, interviews, observation, or tests. A project belongs
here when it can reveal a pattern, test an assumption, measure a change, or
explain a system beyond the reach of routine coverage.

## Reader expectation

Readers should receive a consequential finding and a transparent account of how it was reached. They should be able to inspect the evidence, understand the limits, and separate the reported result from the writer's interpretation.

Every Research piece should make clear:

- the question;
- why the question matters;
- the method;
- the evidence;
- the finding;
- the limitations;
- what should be investigated next.

## What belongs

- Original analysis of a dataset.
- Reporting built from a substantial body of records.
- Interviews that reveal a system or pattern rather than a collection of quotations.
- Original surveys, measurements, tests, or audits conducted with a defensible method.
- Charts and visual explanations that expose a finding.
- Long-form investigations and explanatory projects.
- Replication or careful reanalysis of a claim with public importance.
- A maintained dataset or research tool that makes future reporting possible.

The work must add evidence or analysis that did not exist in the same useful form before publication.

## What does not

- A long article with no original finding.
- A data dump with no question.
- Charts used as decoration.
- A handful of examples presented as a trend.
- A survey with a sample too weak for the conclusion.
- A causal claim drawn from correlation alone.
- Analysis whose method cannot be explained.
- A report commissioned to support a predetermined conclusion.
- Ordinary news reporting extended to fit the section.

## Typical length

The main article usually runs from 1,500 to 4,000 words. Some findings need less. Complex projects may need a series, a methods note, a data appendix, and a public repository.

No fixed ceiling applies. Each additional page, chart, and methodological detail must help a reader understand or inspect the work.

## Tone

Explain the method in plain language and let confidence track the evidence.
Use a technical term when precision requires it, then define it for a reader
outside the field.

The prose should guide the reader through the work without adding drama that
the finding cannot support.

## Publishing philosophy

Set the question and method before analysis. Preserve the source material and
decision record needed for another editor to audit the work.

Publish data and code when rights, privacy, security, and source protection permit. When they do not, explain what has been withheld and why. Document cleaning, exclusions, definitions, transformations, and known gaps. Label estimates and state the assumptions behind them.

Before recruiting participants or collecting personal information, complete
the [research ethics gate](../README.md#research-involving-people). High-risk
work also needs review from someone with relevant subject or methodological
knowledge. Give people and institutions named in consequential findings a fair
chance to respond.

Include a chart, interview, or extra page only when it contributes evidence or
helps the reader inspect the conclusion.

## Success metric

The work succeeds when its finding survives informed scrutiny and remains useful after the publication cycle ends.

Each project should be assessed on:

- whether the evidence supports the stated conclusion;
- whether a qualified reviewer can follow the method;
- whether readers can understand the main finding and its limits;
- whether published data, code, and source notes work as described;
- whether later reporting can build on the work;
- the severity and recurrence of errors, plus the speed and candor of
  corrections;
- whether the project changes an editorial assumption, public understanding, or a relevant decision.

Awards, citations, and traffic may describe reach or influence. The central test remains the integrity and usefulness of the work.

## Internal examples

- Track changes to a platform's public rules over several years. Publish the
  source versions and coding rules beside the finding.
- Test a repeated claim about the cost of a new technology with documented
  prices and a reproducible model. Show how the result changes under reasonable
  assumptions.
- Contracts, filings, public data, and worker interviews reveal where control
  sits inside one supply chain.
- An audit tests popular tools against the privacy promises in their own
  policies. The protocol defines the sample and gives each company a chance to
  respond.
- Archives and interviews reconstruct how a practice moved from a niche
  community into mainstream products.

## Anti-examples

- Three viral posts labeled as evidence of a cultural shift.
- A chart whose scale exaggerates a small change.
- A survey of the publication's own audience generalized to the public.
- A dataset assembled without recording exclusions or duplicates.
- Interviews selected only because they agree with the pitch.
- A conclusion written before the analysis and defended after the method fails.
- A polished interactive that offers no source, method, or inspectable finding.
